item.title: Visualizing Joint Ranking Distributions in Network Meta-Analysis with Hammock Plots
item.description: arXiv:2610.27191v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Treatment ranking provides a summary of the relative effectiveness of competing treatments and is a key output of network meta-analysis (NMA). Existing visualizations primarily summarize marginal ranking distributions or present individual treatment hierarchies with limited insight into uncertainty in the overall hierarchy. We introduce hammock plots as a visualization framework for the joint posterior distribution of treatment rankings. Although motivated by treatment ranking in NMA, the proposed framework is broadly applicable to any setting in which uncertainty in posterior rankings is of interest. Specifically, we develop separate hammock plots to display relationships between (a) adjacent treatments or (b) adjacent ranks. Using highlighting, we show how to assess posterior support for selected treatment hierarchies, to evaluate hierarchies identified by ranking metrics against the posterior distribution, and to examine uncertainty within selected regions of the treatment hierarchy. We apply the proposed visualizations to a thrombolytic treatment network, which revealed patterns in the posterior ranking distribution and the location of uncertainty in treatment hierarchies that were difficult to identify using existing ranking graphics. We also provide a web application to generate all of the proposed hammock plot variations for any data set.
item.dc:creator: Carmen Alicia Liang Zhen, Audrey B\'eliveau, Matthias Schonlau

item.title: Beyond exponential tilting: sharp asymptotics and improved importance sampling for rare events
item.description: arXiv:2610.27434v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A classical approach for importance sampling (IS) of a rare event is to tilt the measure using its large deviation minimizer, thereby shifting the proposal mean towards the event set. While this tilt is log-efficient, we show that the coefficient of variation of the resulting estimator still grows like $\varepsilon^{-1/4}$ in the small-noise limit $\varepsilon\downarrow0$. Motivated by sharp large deviation asymptotics and the local geometry of the event set at the minimizer, we propose improvements using a control variate or an anisotropic, non-Gaussian proposal. We prove, up to truncations that hold with high probability, and confirm empirically in high-dimensional examples, that the former bounds the coefficient of variation and the latter makes it vanish, so that a bounded number of samples suffices. Our analysis addresses both the coefficient of variation of the different proposals and their necessary and sufficient sample size based on the Kullback--Leibler divergence of the IS target from the proposal; both yield the same rates in $\varepsilon$. We demonstrate the resulting samplers, including a variant that blends the classical and the new proposal across noise levels, for a stochastic Korteweg--de Vries equation with thousands of random inputs.
item.dc:creator: Mingxin Li, Hans Reimann, Timo Schorlepp, Georg Stadler

item.title: Geometry-informed importance sampling for rare events
item.description: arXiv:2610.27442v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose GeoIS, a new importance sampling method for estimating rare event probabilities for an underlying Gaussian distribution that exploits asymptotic theory and local event geometry. The proposal distribution is a mixture of two components. The first component draws a Gaussian along the boundary near the instanton and adds to it an exponentially distributed shift into the rare event. This component is derived from the known asymptotic approximation to the optimal zero-variance proposal distribution. The second mixture component is designed to cover missing event mass due to boundary-approximation mismatch, thereby preserving unbiasedness. We rigorously analyze this sampling strategy's performance as a function of event geometry, dimension, rarity level, and number $N$ of importance samples. Under explicit and relatively mild conditions on the former three features, we prove that the squared relative error of GeoIS is bounded by $c/N$ with high probability, for an absolute constant $c$. We implement our method numerically in several examples, including a diffusion PDE problem. The numerical experiments exhibit the qualitative dependence on geometry, dimension, rarity and sample size predicted by the theory, and show that GeoIS markedly outperforms importance sampling methods that use a fully Gaussian proposal distribution.
item.dc:creator: Qinyi Wang, Anya Katsevich, Shanyin Tong

item.title: Practical Advantages of Online Conformal Prediction for Data Streams
item.description: arXiv:2610.27740v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Full conformal prediction offers finite-sample marginal coverage guarantees under exchangeability, but exact computation can be costly, while its classical guarantees do not directly extend to non-stationary data streams. We compare four sequential conformal regression procedures with a weighted full-conformal benchmark in terms of empirical coverage, prediction interval width, and computational cost. The procedures combine ordinary or forgetting-factor least squares with uniform or exponentially weighted empirical residual quantiles, or with online gradient-based quantile tracking. Experiments cover an independent and identically distributed control, two synthetic distribution-shift scenarios, and four real-world data streams. Adapting the regression model as well as the conformal threshold substantially improves the coverage--width tradeoff under drift. The quantile-tracking procedure requires $O(p^2)$ time and memory per observation, independently of stream length, although its coverage can deteriorate after abrupt changes. These results illustrate the practical tradeoffs between predictor adaptation, uncertainty quantification, and computational resources.
item.dc:creator: St\'ephane Chr\'etien, Maryam Hoseini-Behbahani, Guillaume Metzler

item.title: Efficient Bayesian Filtering and Inference for Integro-Difference Equation Models
item.description: arXiv:2610.28170v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Integro-Difference Equation (IDE) models are a class of dynamic spatio-temporal models which describe the temporal evolution of a spatial process, usually to model advection and diffusion of some random field over time. While several papers have focused on inference and performance of these models, little attention has been given to computational comparisons of various methods of computing posterior densities and performing inference. We address this problem in two parts. Firstly, in inference for these models, Kalman filtering (and smoothing) is often used; either to compute marginal likelihoods, or to sample from the hidden process conditional on the rest of the parameters of the model. There are many variations of the Kalman filter and smoother with substantially varying performance profiles and stability: the standard Kalman filter, its square-root form, its information form, to name a few. The information filters, when set up correctly, can compute the likelihood in $\mathcal O(nr^2 + r^3)$ time per time point ($n$ being the number of observations per time point), where the computation in $n$ can be done in parallel, on models with independent observation error. In this paper, we analyse these forms in the context of IDEs, considering computational speed and stability. Secondly, there are two main methods of inference used for the kind of dynamical system that IDEs can be reduced to; directly using the marginal likelihood without the hidden state, or constructing a block Gibbs sampler with the hidden state. We compare these two approaches in terms of computational efficiency and practical performance in the IDE setting. Using a block Gibbs sampler for inference on the system parameters proves to be more efficient in most cases, with a specific real-data example providing an exception.
item.dc:creator: Evan Tate Paterson Hughes, Darren J. Wilkinson, Louis Aslett

item.title: Positive, monotone, and convex Gaussian process regression with Laplacian eigenfunctions
item.description: arXiv:2610.27177v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study how to condition an existing Hilbert space Gaussian process (HSGP) expansion on positivity, monotonicity, or convexity throughout an interval. The expansion has Gaussian coefficients whose variances are given by the kernel's spectral density. At fixed covariance and noise parameters, we retain this coefficient law and represent each complete interval event as a threshold on one coefficient. Integrating out that coefficient gives a strongly log-concave marginal posterior with a normal survival weight, while conditional truncated normal sampling recovers the full constrained law. The construction also covers joint restrictions within the finite expansion. For individual restrictions, we characterize the thresholds through polynomial equations and bound posterior error from conservative numerical evaluation in total variation. Under spectral regularity, the conditioned finite posteriors converge in quadratic Wasserstein distance to the corresponding conditioned underlying GP posteriors as the computational interval expands and higher frequencies are retained. This convergence controls uniform discrepancies in the response and derivatives through the constrained order. Mercury lidar and leaf light-response applications illustrate the consequences for derivative inference.
item.dc:creator: Andreas Kryger Jensen

item.title: Structural equation modelling--based meta-analytic model for diagnostic test accuracy studies
item.description: arXiv:2610.27408v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Bivariate random-effects models are commonly used to jointly synthesize sensitivity and specificity in diagnostic test accuracy (DTA) meta-analysis. However, existing approaches may be sensitive to distributional assumptions and may produce biased estimates of accuracy and between-study heterogeneity with sparse meta-analytic data. We proposed a novel bivariate structural equation modelling (BSEM) approach for DTA meta-analysis and evaluated its performance relative to the bivariate linear mixed model (BLMM) and bivariate generalized linear mixed model (BGLMM). We conducted extensive simulations under varying study, sample-size, accuracy, and heterogeneity conditions. We assessed model performance using bias, root mean squared error (RMSE), confidence interval width, empirical 95% coverage probability (CP), and convergence. We generated study-specific random effects from bivariate normal, t, and Laplace distributions to assess robustness to distributional misspecification. We also applied the models to two empirical DTA datasets. The BSEM generally produced smaller bias and RMSE and nominal-level CP for pooled sensitivity and specificity than the BLMM, while the BGLMM generally yielded results between the two approaches. The BLMM showed stable convergence but tended to underestimate between-study heterogeneity. We observed similar performance patterns under the three random-effects distributions. In the empirical applications, differences between model estimates were generally consistent with patterns observed in the simulations. Overall, the proposed BSEM provided a flexible alternative approach for jointly modelling sensitivity and specificity in DTA meta-analysis, with performance that was generally favourable relative to the BLMM and comparable to the BGLMM across the simulated and empirical settings considered.
item.dc:creator: Zelalem F. Negeri

item.title: Bayesian Neural Networks via Dirichlet Process Priors on the Data-Generating Distribution for Randomized Value Functions in Deep Reinforcement Learning
item.description: arXiv:2610.27570v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) offer a principled framework for quantifying epistemic uncertainty. However, standard weight-space priors yield complex, high-dimensional neural network posteriors that are computationally prohibitive to sample from, and popular approximate inference schemes often fail to capture epistemic uncertainty effectively---a failure mode particularly acute in reinforcement learning (RL) \citep{osband2018randomized}. To resolve this challenge, we introduce a new class of BNNs that quantify uncertainty by placing Bayesian nonparametric Dirichlet Process (DP) priors directly on the underlying data-generating distribution rather than on network parameters. Building on this foundation, we develop DP-DQN, a reinforcement learning algorithm that leverages DP-BNNs to maintain posterior distributions over value functions and perform efficient Thompson sampling. By grounding randomized value functions in Bayesian nonparametrics, DP-DQN unifies data-driven posterior reweighting (via the Bayesian Bootstrap) with generative prior hypotheses injected directly through the DP base measure, enabling decisive ``deep exploration'' with a single neural network without the overhead of multi-network ensembles.
item.dc:creator: Sumit Vashishtha

item.title: Divide-and-Conquer Neural Bayes Estimation for Spatial and Spatiotemporal Point Process Models
item.description: arXiv:2610.27619v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Spatial and spatiotemporal point process models are widely used to analyze event data across many scientific disciplines, but likelihood-based Bayesian inference is often computationally prohibitive due to intractable likelihoods, high-dimensional latent structures, and dependence on event history. Existing approximate and likelihood-free methods mitigate some of these challenges, but often at the cost of reduced statistical efficiency, imperfect uncertainty quantification, or information loss from reliance on predefined summary statistics. A promising recent approach involves neural networks, but it has only been explored in purely spatial or temporal settings and requires a computationally expensive training stage for large domains or dense point patterns. Here, we propose a divide-and-conquer neural Bayes estimation framework for spatial and spatiotemporal point process models. Our method operates directly on raw point pattern realizations using transformer-based architectures on partitions of the spatiotemporal domain, together with an attention mechanism to optimally combine locally extracted summaries. Simulation studies demonstrate reliable inference with improved scalability relative to existing general-purpose neural inference approaches and classical likelihood-based methods. We further demonstrate the practical applicability of our approach through an analysis of whale call data in Cape Cod Bay, MA, where, once trained, the estimator yields parameter estimates and credible intervals at negligible computational cost.
item.dc:creator: Bokgyeong Kang, Andrew Zammit-Mangion, Erin M. Schliep, Robert S. Schick

item.title: Control variates for dry friction under colored noise: variance rates for non-smooth observables
item.description: arXiv:2610.27765v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A control variate method was introduced by Garnier and Mertz (2022) for multivalued stochastic differential equations driven by colored noise. For smooth observables, the asymptotic variance is $O(\varepsilon^{2})$, where $\varepsilon^{2}$ is the correlation time of the noise. However, for non-smooth reliability observables, such as threshold indicators and overshoot severities, rate estimates have not been established in general. In this paper, rate estimates are derived for the inertial dry-friction inclusion driven by colored noise in the three regimes whose white-noise propagators are known. The asymptotic variance of the resulting control variate estimators is $O(\varepsilon^{2\alpha})$ for $\alpha$-H\"older observables with $\alpha\in(0,1]$, $O(\varepsilon)$ for observables of bounded variation satisfying a one-sided continuity condition, $O(\varepsilon^{1+\alpha})$ for observables that are both $\alpha$-H\"older and of bounded variation, and $O(\varepsilon^{\min\{2,1+2\alpha\}})$ for observables with finitely many $\alpha$-cusps, where $\alpha \in (0, 1]$ is the cusp exponent. The last three bounds hold up to logarithmic factors. Bounds on the bias of the white-noise approximation and non-asymptotic sample-size estimates are also derived, and the comparison principle is shown to be preserved under coupled time discretization. Numerical experiments in the three regimes support the predicted rates.
item.dc:creator: Lihong Guo

item.title: Direct Inversion for Chi-Square Sampling, the Squared Bessel Process, and Applications
item.description: arXiv:2412.16655v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In this paper we derive a new direct inversion method to simulate squared Bessel processes. Since the transition probability of these processes can be represented by a non-central chi-square distribution, we construct an efficient and accurate algorithm to simulate non-central chi-square variables. In this method, the dimension of the squared Bessel process, equivalently the degrees of freedom of the chi-square distribution, is treated as a variable. We therefore use a two-dimensional Chebyshev expansion to approximate the inverse function of the central chi-square distribution with one variable being the degrees of freedom. The method is accurate and efficient for any value of degrees of freedom including the computationally challenging case of small values. One advantage of the method is that noncentral chi-square samples can be generated for a whole range of values of degrees of freedom using the same Chebyshev coefficients. This property is especially useful in model calibration. The squared Bessel process is a building block for the well-known Cox-Ingersoll-Ross (CIR) processes, which can be generated from squared Bessel processes through time change and linear transformation. Our direct inversion method thus allows the efficient and accurate simulation of these processes, which are used as models in a wide variety of applications.
item.dc:creator: Simon J. A. Malham, Anke Wiese, Yifan Xu

item.title: Neural Posterior Estimation for Spatial Individual-Level Epidemic Models
item.description: arXiv:2605.29180v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Spatial individual-level models (ILMs) provide a flexible framework for modeling infectious disease transmission across populations with known locations. Bayesian inference for these models relies on Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC), which requires repeated likelihood evaluation and, when parts of the epidemic trajectory are unobserved, data-augmented sampling over high-dimensional latent variables. This computational cost limits the applicability of MCMC to large populations and to settings requiring inference across multiple outbreaks. We propose using neural posterior estimation (NPE) for amortized Bayesian inference in spatial ILMs. NPE trains a conditional normalizing flow on simulated data to approximate the posterior directly, bypassing likelihood evaluation at inference time. We compare two embedding architectures: a convolutional neural network (CNN) operating on the population-level incidence curve and a graph neural network (GNN) operating on individual-level infection and location data. In a simulation study under full observation, stochastic removals, and partial observation, both variants achieve empirical coverage close to the nominal level, with the GNN embedding yielding lower error and narrower credible intervals for the spatial transmission parameters. Data-augmented MCMC is the most accurate when its chains converge, and GNN-NPE is closer to MCMC than CNN-NPE at a small fraction of the per-epidemic cost of MCMC. We apply the framework to the observed 2001 UK foot-and-mouth disease outbreak on 1,177 farms, where MCMC with the exact likelihood provides a reference posterior. Both NPE variants recover the reproduction number estimated by MCMC. GNN-NPE gives a narrower posterior for the spatial decay of transmission than CNN-NPE but is shifted relative to the MCMC reference.
item.dc:creator: Yicheng Mao, Rob Deardon

item.title: Overlapped We Stand, Separated We Fall: Software Approaches to Diagnosing Separation Phenomena in Categorical Response Models
item.description: arXiv:2610.09951v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In statistical models for categorical responses, including binary, nominal and ordinal responses, a phenomenon called ``separation'' may occur which can render maximum likelihood estimate nonexistent and/or nonunique. Based on Sablica et al. (2026)'s general characterization of separation phenomena via structure vectors, in this article we discuss computational, numerical and practical aspects of separation phenomena in different software packages, including consequences, remedies and ways of diagnosing them. We further introduce the R package divoRce which provides the most comprehensive software suite to diagnose separation in existence. It allows to check for separation, to distinguish between types of separation, characterize the recession cone and identify variables and observations contributing to separation for almost any categorical response model in the literature, including models with baseline-category link, cumulative link, adjacent-category link and sequential link specifications. Diagnostics are based on methods for computational geometry and linear programming and can be done in floating-point or rational arithmetic with different solvers. The functionality is easily extendible by wrappers and S3 methods to accommodate implementations in third-party packages or of new categorical response models. We discuss our implementation in detail and show our software in action in a wide range of applications. We recommend to incorporate our checks for separation and existence of the MLE as a diagnostic routine in every categorical data analysis both in third-party software implementations and as part of a standard model diagnostic workflow.
item.dc:creator: Thomas Rusch, Lukas Sablica, Kurt Hornik

item.title: confoundvis for Visualizing and Reporting Sensitivity to Unmeasured Confounding in R
item.description: arXiv:2610.13731v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Sensitivity analysis asks how strong unmeasured confounding would have to be before an observational conclusion changes. Several R packages already calculate established sensitivity quantities, but their outputs use different parameters, objects, and plotting conventions. In this article, we describe confoundvis 0.3.0, an R package designed as a common interface for these analyses. The package stores results from the impact threshold of a confounding variable, the robustness of inference to replacement, partial-R^2 omitted-variable bias analysis, E-values, and Rosenbaum bounds for matched pairs in one confoundsens object. Each result keeps its own parameter and its own published formula. The same functions then draw robustness curves, locate the points at which a conclusion changes, write plain-language reports, and collect several analyses in one table. When a framework describes a confounder by two associations, the package also draws the two-parameter surface on which the familiar single number lies and, where such benchmarks are defined, places measured covariates on the surface. We demonstrate the package with the right heart catheterization data and with a matched-pair study of welders. The native calculations agree with sensemakr, konfound, DOS2, sensitivity2x2xk, and sensitivitymv to numerical or grid precision, and imported EValue results reproduce the reported E-values. The purpose of confoundvis is not to replace the underlying methods or to place their sensitivity parameters on a common scale. Its purpose is to provide a consistent workflow for drawing, comparing, and reporting the results that those methods produce.
item.dc:creator: Subir Hait

item.title: Accuracy of Uniform Inference on Fine Grid Points
item.description: arXiv:2512.18627v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Uniform confidence bands are widely used to quantify uncertainty about unknown functions in nonparametric inference. Although various methods, including the multiplier bootstrap, have been developed and theoretically justified, practical implementations typically replace the supremum over a continuum by the maximum over a finite evaluation grid. This paper investigates how this discretization affects coverage accuracy and how fine the evaluation grid must be to ensure valid uniform inference. We first illustrate through simulations of a kernel-based nonparametric estimator that coarse grids can substantially reduce uniform coverage. Surprisingly, increasing the sample size can worsen coverage on a fixed coarse grid, even as the remaining approximation error on the grid decreases. We then derive general upper bounds on the coverage probability and coverage error of uniform confidence bands based on multiplier-bootstrap critical values on the finite grid points, separating discretization error from the remaining approximation error on the grid. For local empirical processes arising from kernel smoothing, we establish primitive conditions under which coverage converges to zero even when the number of grid points diverges, and conditions ensuring asymptotically nominal coverage. The latter results yield rate-sharp grid resolution requirements in terms of the bandwidth. Furthermore, we derive an explicit leading constant in the bound on coverage error and develop a quantitative grid selection rule for a user-specified discretization tolerance level, which can be implemented through a simple one-dimensional search.
item.dc:creator: Shunsuke Imai
